Yesterday, in Cumberland County, I visited the Harrison Food Bank and Bridgton Hospital to meet the hardworking Mainers working to serve their communities and see how federal funding I secured is helping strengthen important local services.

At the Harrison Food Bank, I enjoyed meeting the dedicated team of volunteers stepping up to help their neighbors in need. It was also rewarding for me to see how the nearly $389,000 I secured helped renovate one of Maine’s largest food banks, expand food assistance to more people, and also create a space for the community to gather and use.

At Bridgton Hospital, I viewed upgraded medical equipment supported by more than $800,000 I secured for Bridgton and Rumford hospitals and received an update on the effort to expand and modernize Bridgton Hospital’s emergency department, a project supported by $5 million I secured earlier this year. In a state as rural as Maine, hospitals like this one are critically important, and I’m so thankful for the doctors, nurses, and staff who work here in Bridgton.

Thank you to the staff and volunteers I met for the important work you do every day to care for your neighbors.

It was great to visit Mid-Maine Technical Center in Waterville today to meet with students and instructors and to see several of the center’s programs in action, including the new engineering and manufacturing program that is supported by more than $700,000 in federal funding I secured to purchase new machine tooling, 3D metal printing, and other equipment.

Seeing students work directly with advanced equipment and apply what they’re learning in real time shows how this kind of hands-on training helps prepare students well for careers in high-skilled, competitive fields. I was especially impressed to meet students in the nursing program who are on track to earn their certified nursing assistant credentials before graduating, helping address pressing workforce needs in Maine.

As Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, I will continue to support initiatives aimed at improving workforce training in our state.

Today in York County, I visited community development projects supported by a combined $5.3 million in federal funding I secured, including both a substance use disorder treatment center and a first responder training facility. Days like today are a terrific reminder of all the good that is possible for our state when seniority on the Appropriations Committee is used to deliver targeted funding for tangible, lasting improvements in communities where they would otherwise be out of reach.

With these projects, Alfred and the greater York County community will have expanded access to substance use disorder treatment to address the negative effects of the opioid and fentanyl crises, as well as a dedicated facility to train more firefighters, police officers, and EMS professionals to better keep our communities safe. These two projects are clear examples of the federal government working for Maine people, and I am glad I was able to secure this funding to help make them a reality.

B001257.text: The newly released House Budget includes $2.1 million for a project I was proud to sponsor - an investment that will bring one of the most advanced neuroimaging platforms in the nation into an already world-class, interdisciplinary research and care environment.  Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s are not inevitable consequences of aging. They are complex biological processes that can be visualized, measured, and ultimately changed. The 7T MRI platform is the most powerful noninvasive technology available today, capable of imaging the human brain at near-histologic resolution. It serves as a critical bridge between scientific discovery and real-world treatments. This funding will help ensure the United States remains at the forefront of neurodegenerative disease research — accelerating progress toward better treatments, stronger prevention strategies, and, ultimately, cures for patients and families who need them most.

I’m proud to share that the newly released House Budget includes $3,000,000 I sponsored to support the Sustainable Futures Program in Pasco County.  This innovative K-12 initiative is designed to prepare the next generation of leaders by focusing on sustainability, including: water supply, water quality and conservation, agriculture, and natural resource management.  Through Environmental Problem-Based Learning, students will take part in immersive, hands-on experiences that bring classroom lessons to life and connect them to real-world environmental challenges.  In partnership with the Southwest Florida Water Management District, and through field-based learning on conserved lands right here in Pasco, students will gain a deeper understanding of how to responsibly manage our natural resources.  By investing in education and stewardship today, we are building a stronger, more sustainable future for our community and beyond.

I’m proud to introduce the Developing the Community Health Workforce Act - a bipartisan effort to strengthen our healthcare workforce and expand access to high-quality care nationwide.  Federally Qualified Community Health Centers  (FQHCs) are on the frontlines, serving millions of Americans.   They are a proven success story and a vital part of what’s working in our healthcare system.  

As Co-Chair of the Community Health Center Caucus, I’ve long worked to secure increased support for FQHCs. This legislation builds on that effort by strengthening the workforce pipeline, supporting recruitment and retention, and ensuring providers have the tools they need to deliver high-quality, patient-centered care.  By investing in these trusted, community-based models, we can improve health outcomes and build a stronger, more resilient healthcare system for all.

On Tuesday, the House Appropriations Committee voted on the Fiscal Year 2027 Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies funding bill. However, there are a few areas where I feel that the bill falls short in providing for our servicemembers, veterans, and their families. Access to quality healthcare is one of the most important ways we can support members of the armed forces. This bill does not do enough to give veterans access to the timely healthcare that they deserve, and it lacks the accountability needed to make sure that taxpayers’ dollars are being spent responsibly.

I look forward to working with my colleagues on both sides of the aisle to produce a final bill that best supports the needs of our veteran and military communities.

C001053.text:
We just ended the Democrat-led Department of Homeland Security shutdown.

This funding bill fully restores funding, stability, and pay for the majority of critical operations including TSA, FEMA, Secret Service, Coast Guard, and CISA – and it does so without any policy restrictions at the center of Chuck Schumer and Senate Democrats’ radical agenda.

While the far-left hoped to eradicate U.S. Border Patrol and Immigration and Customs Enforcement resources, complete funding for those agencies is advancing concurrently. This two-pronged approach restores DHS immediately and makes it clear: enforcement will not be stripped.

Having Democrats diminish Article I and force the use of reconciliation was not my preferred path. Yet, this is the reality before us. My support of today’s action is for all the frontline personnel who would have – once again – been subjected to missed paychecks starting this weekend. I’d rather carry the weight of an imperfect move forward than ask them to carry the real-life burden of Democrat failure.

Trying to unilaterally dictate which national security functions survive while holding key operations and employees hostage during the longest government shutdown in history is not a record I would be proud of – but it’s one Democrats hold.

I thoroughly regret the erosion of the appropriations process Senate Democrats have instigated, and the consequences that were paid by everyday Americans. It is not a standard I accept – and my votes and position throughout this process have made that clear, each and every time.

In July of 2024, while President Trump was campaigning in Butler, Pennsylvania, a gunman fired at the President. As the bullet grazed his ear on live television, I, as well as most Americans, were left in a state of disbelief and shock. This attempted assassination was chilling. It was a horrific attack of democracy and was just simply un-American.

This was an event I hoped our nation would never experience again. Yet, just two months later, authorities reported another attempted assassination of the President. In September of 2024, a man was spotted hiding in the bushes with a rifle aiming at the golf course where President Trump was golfing in Florida. Luckily, a Secret Service agent engaged the suspect before President Trump came into the shooter’s view. Nonetheless, it was another attempted attack on our President and, therefore, our nation.

Then, this weekend, a gunman with multiple weapons stormed the event venue of the White House Correspondents Dinner. Shots were fired, one of our brave Secret Service agents was hit, and the attacker left behind a manifesto claiming all Trump Administration officials, excluding one, were his targets. Luckily, no one was injured. However, the fact of the matter is this: this is the third time in less than two years that President Trump has faced an assassination attempt.

This should make every American, regardless of their political views, stop and reflect on the condition of our current culture and why this is happening.

Political violence is never acceptable – and I truly do believe the majority of Americans instinctively reject political violence. Most of us know what happened on Saturday night is wrong. Yet, as we reflect on this horrific event, we ought to think about what this political violence represents. To me, it symbolizes a deeper problem within our own society, culture, and political system.

Political rhetoric in our country has gotten out of hand. I am not naïve. I know that reckless rhetoric is not a tactic used by just one political party. However, today, I am speaking about the three assassination attempts on President Trump.

When I hear politicians compare the President to Hitler or compare federal law enforcement agencies like Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol to Nazi Germany’s Gestapo and SS, I am appalled. Anyone who has read the history books knows how false and out of touch with reality those comparisons are. Moreover, it should be obvious that such rhetoric is dangerous. In fact, this kind of rhetoric is exactly what fuels the unstable and violence prone members of our society to act.

So, while I do think there will be almost a universal rejection by elected officials of the violence that occurred at the event on Saturday, I encourage all elected officials to think more deeply. I encourage them to stop and look at their own rhetoric when speaking about the President and their other political opponents. If that language is provocative, they ought to correct it immediately. Furthermore, I urge all American citizens to condemn politicians – from either party – who use problematic language when talking about the President, federal agencies, or other politicians. Dangerous rhetoric must end immediately.

The second thing we ought to remember is that many of the law enforcement officials who bravely and swiftly acted to protect the President, Vice President, our Cabinet members, and many of my colleagues on Saturday night are currently operating under an agency that is not funded. The events at the White House Correspondents Dinner this weekend demonstrate just how unacceptable it is to fail to fund the government, particularly the Department of Homeland Security, during this time of threats from abroad and political turmoil at home.

It is a huge mistake not to fund DHS and the selfless law enforcement agents who work within that agency. We should never, ever close an agency that protects not just the President, but every American citizen. It is unacceptable and reckless.

Finally, I want to make this clear: the House, under the leadership of Speaker Johnson, has voted to fully fund DHS five separate times. It is the Senate that has failed to do so – and not because the majority of the Senate doesn’t favor it. In fact, the majority of both chambers have voted to fund the Department of Homeland Security repeatedly. The hold up during this time of threats to our nation is all because of the misuse of a Senate rule, the filibuster. This is an issue I will delve into deeper during a later column.

So, what do we, as a nation, do now? In this moment, we should correct dangerous political rhetoric, move to immediately fund the agencies that keep us safe, and unite as a nation. We must not allow these types of horrific attacks to persist. As President Trump said in his statement after the assassination attempt in Butler, we must “show our True Character as Americans, remaining Strong and Determined.”

The United States of America is the greatest country this Earth has ever known. We must not allow evil from within to undermine our traditions of peaceful dissent and respect for those who hold opposing political views. Surely that is something that all Americans, regardless of party, can accept, celebrate, and practice when engaged in political debate and discussion.

My thoughts and prayers are with the President, my colleagues, and everyone who was put in danger at the White House Corespondents dinner tonight. Thank you to the Secret Service and law enforcement for their swift and brave action. Political violence is never acceptable.

Inflation continues to raise costs for groceries, gas, child care, and other essentials, putting added pressure on families across South Texas. That’s why I’m an original cosponsor of the American Family Act to expand the Child Tax Credit and help parents keep more money in their pockets each month.

The American Family Act would ensure the expanded and improved Child Tax Credit is made permanent, giving families more breathing room to cover everyday expenses and keep up with rising costs. Under the American Family Act, no child would lose access to the full Child Tax Credit simply because their family earns too little.

Unfortunately, under the current Child Tax Credit in #TX28, 94,000 children, or 45%, will not qualify for the full credit. Income restrictions in the current Child Tax Credit also prevent poorer families from receiving the full credit.

Many Hispanic families face additional barriers tied to concentration in lower-paid occupations, resulting in nearly 42% of Hispanic children nationwide not receiving the full credit in 2026. Across Texas, higher-income households receive a larger share of the credit, while families in the lowest income bracket receive an average of just $113 under current law. More than a quarter of children in those households don’t qualify for the full credit.

With the American Family Act, the lowest-income households in Texas could receive up to $4,700, while ensuring every child qualifies for the full credit regardless of how much their parents earn.

I’ll keep working to deliver for South Texas families and build bipartisan support for solutions that help parents manage rising costs and give every child the support they need to succeed.

Honored to participate in the dedication ceremony of the Corporal Michael D. Anderson Jr. Post Office Building.  The post office in his hometown of Modesto is named to honor and memorialize his life, service, patriotism, heroism, and ultimate sacrifice.

Michael Anderson Jr. grew up in Modesto.  In 2001, he graduated from Johansen High School.  After the September 11 terror attacks that year, he bravely answered his nation’s call to service by enlisting in the Marine Corps, where he quickly became a leader and distinguished himself.

He was a member of the Fleet Antiterrorism Security Teams, or FAST Company, an elite Marine Corp team designed to fight terror around the world.  He received a letter of commendation from the U.S. Ambassador.  In September 2004, Corporal Anderson deployed to Iraq.  Eleven days before Christmas, on December 14, 2004, he was tragically killed in action.  He was twenty-one years old.

Corporal Anderson showed tremendous bravery and courage as reflected by his two Purple Hearts, the Marine Corps Achievement Medal with the “V” for Valor as well as the Combat Action Ribbon and many other award citations.

I was proud to carry legislation to rename the post office located at 2300 Sylvan Avenue in Modesto to the “Corporal Michael D. Anderson Jr. Post Office Building."

In recent weeks I've been talking with President Trump's administration about my effort to extend the moratorium on regulations that could cripple our state's iconic lobster industry. Today, we got word that he will support my bill. 

The need to protect this key Maine industry knows no party. I’m grateful for the President’s support for Maine’s lobstermen and hopeful that my colleagues in the House will join me in quickly passing this bill into law.

Today is International Workers Day and I’m celebrating by working to strengthen the collective bargaining process to ensure union workers don’t have to wait to get the fair contracts they deserve.

Today, a loophole in federal labor law means that even after workers vote to form a union, the fight’s not over. Companies drag their feet on negotiations, hoping to break the union. On average, it takes 458 days to obtain a first contract. That’s far too long. 

The Faster Labor Contracts Act would establish clear deadlines for a first contract, and guarantee mediation and binding arbitration if the deadlines aren’t met. That will incentivize good-faith negotiation on a fair timeline. 

I’m a co-sponsor of this bill and I just signed @DonaldNorcross's Discharge Petition to start the process of forcing the Speaker to give us a vote on the floor. 

Solidarity Forever.

Affordability is top of mind for South Carolinians, and we’re making it a priority in Congress.

We’ve introduced legislation to hold Washington accountable for driving up the cost of living and to tackle the housing crisis so more South Carolinians can achieve homeownership.

The American Family Cost-of-Living Relief Act of 2026: Federal agencies must publish an initial household cost impact analysis alongside any proposed rule covering housing, utilities, food, healthcare, transportation, childcare, education, and more. After the public comment period, agencies must publish a final updated cost impact analysis. Any rule projected to substantially increase household costs, by $50 or more per year, is blocked from taking effect unless required by law or certified as necessary to address a national security emergency or presidentially declared disaster.

The Making Homeownership Affordable Again Act: Eliminates capital gains taxes on the sale of primary residences and on any home sold to a first-time buyer, unlocking more housing supply and keeping more money in the pockets of hardworking South Carolinians.

The First-Time Homebuyer Savings Act of 2026: Creates tax-advantaged savings accounts, allowing first-time buyers to contribute up to $10,000 per year in pre-tax funds, which can grow and be withdrawn tax-free for qualifying home purchase expenses.

The FAIR Labels Act will establish a federal guideline for labeling cell-cultivated and plant-based alternative protein products, ensuring consumers can easily differentiate these products from real beef products produced by U.S. cattlemen and cattlewomen. We thank these members of the House and Senate for their efforts to protect truthful beef labeling and deliver clarity in the marketplace.” – Gene Copenhaver, President of @BeefUSA

R to @RepRonnyJackson: “Texas Farm Bureau (TFB) appreciates Congressman Ronny Jackson’s leadership on the Fair and Accurate Ingredient Representation (FAIR) on Labels Act. This legislation is an important step toward ensuring transparency in the marketplace, protecting the integrity of real meat products, and preventing consumers from being misled. We urge Congress to pass this legislation.” – Russell Boening, President of @TexasFarmBureau

R to @RepRonnyJackson: “Food labels should be clear and avoid any attempt to mislead, confuse or misrepresent what is included in the product. The FAIR Labels Act requires USDA and FDA to develop food product definitions that will alleviate consumer confusion and provide certainty that the labels on the food we purchase are truthful. TCFA appreciates Rep. Jackson for his work and leadership on this important issue that will benefit beef consumers and cattle producers.” – Laphe LaRoe, Chairman of @txcattlefeeders

Today, the House passed a new farm bill, bringing certainty and support to farmers and ranchers after years of extensions. Backed by over 500 stakeholder groups, the bill strengthens risk management tools, boosts domestic production, supports American specialty crops, and modernizes rural programs, all while staying budget neutral and solidifying nearly $200 billion in SNAP reform.

Tonight, I voted to reauthorize and reform FISA Section 702 with even stronger protections, accountability, and transparency, balancing critical Fourth Amendment rights with the need to protect against foreign enemies and attacks. In today’s world, this is a difficult balance. But we need our government to be able to act quickly against foreign threats while ensuring it does not invade the fundamental privacy rights of citizens.

Two years ago, we made 56 reforms to FISA. Those reforms have resulted in 94% fewer database queries since 2022, along with heightened criminal accountability for anyone who misuses the database and stricter oversight. We expanded on that today, clarifying that no U.S. persons can be targeted through FISA without a judicial warrant. Additionally, the bill requires the Government Accountability Office to audit current targeting procedures and directs the Attorney General to issue procedures allowing Members of Congress and their staff to access FISA hearings. 

I will continue working to ensure agencies have the tools to protect against foreign attacks while maintaining Congress’s Article I oversight authority and preventing executive branch abuse.

I voted against an appropriations bill amendment earlier this year being labeled a “kill switch” vote. What I actually voted for was a study of development of passive impaired driving prevention technology, along with clear guardrails to protect drivers. What’s being discussed is early-stage, in-vehicle technology that would operate passively and independently.

H001100.text:
Today is National Nurses Day, and I want to recognize the nurses across Western and Southern Colorado who serve our communities every day.

From hospitals and clinics to schools and long-term care facilities, nurses are often there during life’s most difficult moments. They play an essential role in keeping our healthcare system running and ensuring patients and families receive the care they need.

Earlier today, I stopped by Community Hospital to thank a few nurses in person for the work they do every day to care for patients across the Western Slope.

Their compassion, professionalism, and steady commitment help keep #CO03 healthy and strong. Thank you for serving our communities with such exceptional care and dedication.

Yesterday, I joined Secretary of Veterans Affairs Doug Collins at Colorado Mesa University for a roundtable with veterans, VA leaders, and community partners from across Western Colorado.

We heard directly from veterans about the challenges many still face navigating the VA system, especially during the transition to civilian life, accessing benefits, and communicating with the VA. We also discussed mental health support, improving access to care, and modernizing the VA’s systems to better serve veterans and their families.

#CO03 is home to thousands of veterans, and these conversations are critical to ensuring they receive the care and support they have earned through their service.

Thank you to Secretary Collins for visiting Grand Junction and to the veterans who shared their experiences and perspectives today. @SecVetAffairs

Last week, the Science, Space, and Technology Committee advanced bipartisan legislation focused on quantum technology and America’s long-term competitiveness.

Quantum research will shape the future of computing, cybersecurity, communications, and national defense. The countries that lead in these technologies will have major economic and strategic advantages in the decades ahead.

Colorado is already at the forefront, with world-class universities, researchers, and national labs driving innovation right here in our state.

My focus is making sure the United States stays ahead and that communities like #CO03 benefit from the jobs, investment, and technological leadership that come with it.

Thank you, Secretary Collins, for visiting the Grand Junction VA and hearing directly from veterans and providers in Western Colorado.

We discussed the importance of timely, reliable care for veterans across our large rural district and making sure those who served can access the benefits they’ve earned without unnecessary delays.

Helping veterans navigate the VA remains a core focus of my office. #CO03

On National Teacher Appreciation Day, we recognize the educators across #CO03 who invest in our students and strengthen our communities.

I am especially thankful for teachers go the extra mile to bring their students to Washington D.C. to give them firsthand understanding of our nation’s capital and how our government works.

Their commitment shapes the next generation, and their impact is felt far beyond the classroom. Thank you for all that you do.

During my first year in Congress, I secured $20,731,975 that will support seven communities in our 2nd District for water infrastructure, public safety, health care, and education initiatives. The Farm Bill the House passed last week can give Kansas farmers the ability to plan for years to come--no more year-to-year uncertainty. That's why I supported it. There's plenty of risk inherent in production agriculture, so we need to control what we can control.

Our office met with leadership in Rota to discuss the island’s ongoing recovery efforts following Super Typhoon Sinlaku. 

Conversations focused on community needs, the condition of essential services and infrastructure, and the support needed to help families and local businesses continue recovering. 

While Rota experienced less damage than some neighboring islands, the importance of continued coordination and recovery support remains critical for the community moving forward.

Discussions focused on the immediate challenges facing the island’s power infrastructure, the support needed for recovery, and the importance of strengthening systems to better withstand future storms. 

We remain committed to working alongside local leaders and utility crews to help ensure reliable services are restored for the people of Tinian.

Our office visited the Tinian Health Center to assess storm related damage and meet with the healthcare professionals continuing to serve the community during recovery efforts.

We discussed the challenges they are facing, the condition of the facility, and the resources needed to maintain essential medical services for residents.

Even under difficult circumstances, their dedication to caring for the people of Tinian continues to show the strength and resilience of the island.

Our office met with local leadership in Tinian to assess the impact left behind by the storm.
